title: Large Language Models in Peer-Run Community Behavioral Health Services: Understanding Peer Specialists and Service Users’ Perspectives on Opportunities, Risks, and Mitigation Strategies

bias_targets.methodology: Qualitative evaluation through comicboarding workshops where peer specialists and service users identified that LLM recommendations often assume middle-class privileges (e.g., access to transportation, stable housing, and cell phones) while ignoring the systemic barriers and severe resource limitations faced by disadvantaged populations.

Qualitative co-design workshops eliciting stakeholder feedback on how LLMs default to medicalized, diagnostic terminology and frameworks (e.g., "patient", "treatment") rather than the person-centered, trauma-informed, and recovery-oriented language used in peer-run communities.

Qualitative analysis of participant feedback highlighting how LLMs fail to use person-first or person-led language regarding physical and psychiatric disabilities, risking the reinforcement of mental health stigma and the misinterpretation of trauma responses as pathology.
